title: Probe injection and graceful fallback playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc is an operational playbook that combines small-scale probe injection (intentional traffic probes to validate routing safety), failure-drain patterns, and graceful fallback procedures for control-plane and multi-region routing incidents. It is intentionally pragmatic — half architecture notes, half runbook steps — and meant for on-call engineers and platform SREs who need a deterministic process to detect, validate, and recover routing/control-plane regressions without cascading user-visible impact.

Scope & assumptions:
- Applies to routing/control-plane tiers that decide model routing, region steering, and capacity tiering (hosted/dedicated/private ceilings).
- Assumes standard observability: request metrics (rps, errors), model-level latency (p50/p95), routing-decision logging, region capacity metrics, and traces are available in the Console.
- Assumes access to rdctl (internal runtime control CLI), k8s cluster admin for the control-plane pods, and permission to modify routing policy feature flags and canaries.
- This is NOT a substitute for product-level rollbacks; it focuses on infrastructure routing and fallback.

Quick glossary (keeps us aligned):
- Probe: synthetic request injected with test user header x-rd-probe: true that should follow standard routing decisions and be logged in tracing.
- Soft-fallback: route traffic to a compatible model variant or lower-cost region but keep original routing decisions in logs for diagnostics.
- Hard-fallback: immediate switch to a pre-approved fallback endpoint/region (use only if soft-fallback fails or latency/error SLOs breached).
- Drain window: temporary traffic reduction to problematic region/component while keeping a small sample for validation (default 5-10% for 10 minutes).

Detection thresholds (operational):
- Error rate: sustained 3% errors (5xx) for model endpoints across any region for >= 3 minutes.
- Latency: p95 crosses region SLO (200ms for small chat paths, 600ms for long generation) for >= 5 minutes.
- Decision divergence: >1% of probes receive a different routing decision compared to control baseline in 2 consecutive 1-minute windows.
- Capacity alarm: region capacity utilization > 88% (GPU queue length rising) with evictions or pod OOMs.

Pre-incident prep (do this before injecting probes or runbook use):
- Verify runbook ownership oncall roster and primary/secondary.
- Ensure a small canary namespace/flag exists for probe traffic: rdctl flags create probe-canary --allow-probe-routing=true
- Confirm telemetry endpoints: probe-traces, routing-decision-sink, model-qps-dashboard.
- Short list fallback variants per model with explicit compatibility notes in the product catalog.

Probe injection pattern (safe, incremental):
1) Small smoke probes (non-impacting): 1 rps per region for 2 minutes. Check traces and routing logs.
   - rdctl probe send --region us-west1 --model gpt-small --headers "x-rd-probe:true" --count 120
2) Decision-consistency probes: run parallel probes against a control region to assert deterministic routing decisions.
   - rdctl probe compare --src us-east1 --dst us-west1 --model gpt-medium --count 200 --compare-fields routing_hash,variant
3) Load-proportional probes: only after step 1/2 succeed, ramp to 5-10 rps per region for 5 minutes to validate scaling paths.

Incident scenario A: regional routing drift detected (decision divergence)
Symptoms:
- Pager: routing-decision-divergence-alert
- Observed: >1% probes show different routing decisions; subtle variant mismatch; possibly due to feature-flag desync or control-plane version skew.
Immediate steps:
1) Acknowledge pager, post to #oncall-platform with incident-key: RD-<timestamp>.
2) Run targeted probe comparison across regions and nodes: rdctl probe compare --src us-east1 --dst eu-west1 --model <affected> --count 500. Save logs.
3) Check control-plane gitops status: kubectl -n controlplane get pod -o wide; check image tags and reconcile drift with git repo.
4) If a feature-flag push occurred in last 15 minutes, temporarily toggle the flag off: rdctl flags set routing-experiment-42=false and re-evaluate.
Mitigation (soft-first):
- Apply a soft-fallback route rule for affected customer cohorts: rdctl routing apply --policy fallback-soft --target-region eu-west1 --pct 10 --duration 10m
- Keep 1% probe traffic routed through original path for diagnostics; do NOT disable logs.
Escalation to hard-fallback:
- If divergence stays >1% after 15 minutes and customer P0s are observed, execute hard-fallback: rdctl routing set-global-fallback --region us-east1 --use-solid-variant=gpt-medium-qual1
Post-incident tasks:
- Create JIRA INFRA-xxxx with timeline, root cause hypothesis, and model routing decision samples.
- Schedule a postmortem with product owners if customer-visible.

Incident scenario B: control-plane instability causing intermittent routing failures
Symptoms:
- Control-plane pods crashlooping or APIs 500ing; routing RPCs timing out; sudden uptick in routing timeouts in traces.
Immediate steps:
1) Confirm control-plane health: kubectl -n controlplane get pods; kubectl logs -f pod/control-api-abc --since=10m.
2) Isolate recent deploys: kubectl rollout history deployment/control-api; if last deploy within 30 minutes, consider rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-api --to-revision=<prev>
3) If rollback is not immediately possible, scale out read-only control-plane replicas to reduce load: kubectl scale deployment/control-api --replicas=5
Safe traffic drain:
- Begin a controlled region drain to reduce load: rdctl routing apply --drain-region=us-east1 --pct=60 --preserve-probe=1
- Monitor measure: errors and traces should drop within 2x loop time (30s).
If pods continue failing:
- Increase isolation: switch routing to fallback-region using hard-fallback policy (see command above).

Incident scenario C: multi-region overload (capacity evaporation)
Symptoms:
- Queue length per-GPU increases, backpressure seen in frontend, compute autoscaler not keeping up.
Immediate steps:
1) Identify overloaded regions: dashboards -> capacity -> GPU queue length.
2) Activate cross-region burst policy for 30 minutes: rdctl autoscale cross-region-burst --from-region=eu-west1 --to-region=us-central1 --max-pct=25
3) If burst policy fails: lower model batch size profile as temporary mitigation (affects cost/quality): rdctl models set-profile --model gpt-large --profile low-latency
4) As last resort, apply emergency rate-limit for non-critical tenants: rdctl quotas set --tenant-group=platinum-sandbox --qps=10 --duration=1h

Common safe commands (cheat sheet):
- rdctl probe send --region <r> --model <m> --headers "x-rd-probe:true" --count <n>
- rdctl routing apply --policy fallback-soft --target-region <r> --pct <10> --duration 10m
- rdctl routing set-global-fallback --region <r> --use-solid-variant=<variant-id>
- kubectl -n controlplane logs <pod> --since=5m
- kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-api --to-revision=<rev>

Rollout safety knobs & post-change validation:
- After any routing/policy change wait 120s then run a 200-probe compare against a control region.
- Maintain an audit log tag on changes: rdctl change tag --ticket JIRA-xxxx --reason "soft-fallback for controlplane instability"
- For every emergency hard-fallback create a follow-up ticket and attach routing decision samples and the probe trace IDs.

Escalation matrix (timing is approximate):
- 0-5 minutes: primary oncall (platform) acts, post Slack, run probes.
- 5-15 minutes: secondary oncall joins, coordinate rollback/fallback.
- 15+ minutes: Eng leads + SRE manager join, consider customer comms and scheduled maintenance.

Postmortem & remediation checklist:
- Collect traces, routing decisions, and probe logs into the incident ticket.
- Correlate with control-plane deploys and feature flag changes.
- Add deterministic unit/integration test for failure mode (if control-plane bug).
- Update the model catalog compatibility matrix if fallback mismatches were discovered.
- Run a targeted chaos test in staging to validate fix (probe-injection with simulated partial-network).

Notes to on-call / quick tips:
- Don’t flip many flags at once. If uncertain, prefer soft-fallbacks and throttled drains.
- Preserve trace IDs for at least 7 days when probes are used for incident evidence.
- Prefer routing rules that are reversible and have a ttl/duration.

Appendix: example incident timeline (realistic template)
- 09:02: Pager: routing-decision-divergence-alert triggered (1.7% probes divergent).
- 09:04: Primary ack, started rdctl probe compare, saw majority of divergence tied to feature flag routing-experiment-42.
- 09:09: Toggled feature flag off; diversion dropped to 0.2% within 2 minutes.
- 09:25: Post-incident: created JIRA INFRA-2112, assigned to Daniel Park for root-cause analysis.

Appendix: test matrix for probe scenarios (staging only)
- Test 1: routing-decision consistency, 1 rps x 30m, measure deterministic hash equality.
- Test 2: control-plane version skew, staggered deploys across regions and assert stable decisions.
- Test 3: failover timing, simulate pod crash and validate probe-based hard-fallback completes in <120s.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Add automated rollback hook into RDCTL to allow single-command rollback to last known-good routing policy.
- Formalize customer-facing throttles per-seat vs global throttles.
- Improve telemetry to mark probe vs production without polluting billing metrics.

If you’re the oncall: copy this doc into the incident ticket, paste command output into the ticket and call out steps you took. Ping the platform slack channel with the incident key and primary mitigation action.

End of document.
